lines.say: Tonight, after you turn off the light, your house gets a whole new crew.
One of them hunts the others in the dark. And one is on your face right now.
So Meatball stayed up all night with a flashlight, to watch the night shift.
And we'll get to the worst one at five AM.

_sources: CT Ag. Experiment Station, Silverfish and Firebrats fact sheet
Univ. of Maryland, Bug of the Week: Ancient insect in a modern world (2021)

lines.say: Ten PM. Lights off. First one out: the silverfish.
It hates light, so it spends the day in cracks, and waits for dark.
Meatball clicked on his flashlight. Gone. Straight back into the crack.
It's out for starch. Book glue, paper, cereal, wallpaper paste.
It can take two years to grow up, and it keeps shedding its skin its whole life.
Its cousin, the firebrat, goes for the warmest spot in the house, right by your furnace.
And its family is ancient. Silverfish-like insects were around before the dinosaurs.
But silverfish are the easy ones. At eleven, the kitchen gets crowded.

_sources: Univ. of Kentucky Entomology, Cockroach Control Manual (ENTFACT-614)
Jayaram & Full 2016, PNAS (UC Berkeley News)
Scientific American, Fact or fiction: a cockroach can live without its head

lines.say: Eleven PM. The kitchen opens for business. Cockroaches.
They hide in cracks all day, and come out at night to eat almost anything you leave out.
A German cockroach egg case can hatch up to forty babies.
And one German roach can turn into thousands in under a year.
They can squeeze through a crack about as thin as two stacked pennies.
Meatball tried to step on one. It can survive nine hundred times its own weight pressing down.
Meatball stepped harder. It can even live for weeks without its head.
But the real danger is what it leaves behind. Droppings and shed skins can trigger asthma, especially in kids.
Meatball checked the clock. Eleven fifteen. It was going to be a long night.
And something with fifteen pairs of legs is already on its way.

_sources: Penn State Extension, House Centipedes
CT Ag. Experiment Station, House Centipede fact sheet
Frontiers in Zoology (2024), leg autotomy
Penn State Extension, House Centipedes (origin, 1849)

lines.say: Midnight. The hunter wakes up. The house centipede.
Up to fifteen pairs of legs. And it didn't come for you. It came for the cockroaches.
It runs them down, and eats them. Silverfish too. Even bed bugs.
It's not even from here. It came from around the Mediterranean, and was seen in Pennsylvania as early as 1849.
So if you keep seeing them, they've found food. You may have other bugs.
Grab it by a leg, and the leg pops right off. It's built to break.
Can it bite? Rarely, mostly if you grab it. It can hurt, but it isn't considered dangerous.
Meatball gave it a trophy. Employee of the night.
Then, around one, the walls start scratching.

_sources: UC IPM Pest Notes: House Mouse (Pub. 7483)
CDC, How to Clean Up After Rodents

lines.say: One AM. Scratching, inside the wall. The house mouse.
Mice are busiest at night, and they don't even need to drink. They get water from your food.
So it's eating your snacks, and drinking them too.
It chews through wires, and it can squeeze through a gap about the width of a pencil.
It also chews gas lines and appliance cords. And a female can have up to ten litters a year.
And it rarely goes more than thirty feet from its nest. So if you see one, the nest is close.
Found droppings? Don't sweep them dry. The CDC says soak them with disinfectant first, with gloves on.
Next comes the calmest creature of the night. After that, it gets a lot worse.

_sources: Missouri Dept. of Conservation, Life on a Thread (2024)
Rößler et al. 2022, PNAS, REM-like sleep in jumping spiders

lines.say: Two AM. On your window, something is sleeping. A jumping spider.
Big front eyes, and no web at all. In the daytime it stalks bugs on your windowsill, then pounces.
Some can leap up to forty times their own body length.
Some jumping spiders hang from a single silk thread, all night.
And scientists filmed its eyes twitching, in a sleep-like state. And scientists wonder if it might even be dreaming.
Meatball tucked it in.

_sources: Burke Museum, Spider Myths
Scientific American (2014), Fact or fiction: we swallow spiders in our sleep
Missouri Dept. of Conservation, Cellar Spiders
UC Riverside Spider Research (R. Vetter)

lines.say: Three AM. The question everybody asks. Do spiders crawl into your mouth while you sleep?
That eight spiders a year thing? Spider experts say there's no evidence for it. At all.
To a spider, a sleeping human is a giant, breathing, rumbling mountain. Most stay far away.
Ever see a skinny spider in a ceiling corner? A cellar spider. It eats bugs, and other spiders too.
But something else really is in your bed tonight. And it wants your blood.

_sources: Univ. of Kentucky Entomology, Bed Bugs (ENTFACT-636)
US EPA, Bed Bugs: Appearance and Life Cycle
CDC, About Bed Bugs
Univ. of Kentucky ENTFACT-636 (eggs, starvation, travel)

lines.say: Four AM. If you have bed bugs, this is feeding time. They bite while you sleep.
They find you by your breath. The carbon dioxide you breathe out helps guide them to you.
A bite takes a few minutes, and you usually don't feel a thing.
Then they crawl back into the seams of your mattress, and hide.
Their eggs are about the size of a speck of dust.
They hitch a ride home in your luggage, your bags, and your folded clothes.
And in the cold, they can wait up to a year between meals.
Meatball tried sleeping with the flashlight on. They don't care. They still come out.
The CDC says they're not known to spread disease. Bites may itch, or you may feel nothing.
But the grossest one isn't in your bed. It's on your face.

_sources: Smith et al. 2022, Molecular Biology and Evolution (Univ. of Reading release)
Thoemmes et al. 2014, PLOS ONE

lines.say: Five AM. The grossest one. It's on your face, right now. Face mites.
They're called Demodex. They live in the pores of your face, eating the oil.
Each one is about a third of a millimeter long. Way too small to see.
Scientists tested adults, and found mite DNA on every single person they tested.
And at night, they move between your pores, on your face, to find a mate.
Meatball has washed his face eleven times since he found this out.
Good news: they're normal, and usually harmless. They're just very, very close.
And when your alarm goes off, one crew still won't leave.

segments.chapter: 6 AM: the ones that never leave
_sources: American Lung Association, Dust Mites
AAAAI, Dust Mite Allergy
AAAAI: keep indoor humidity below 50%

lines.say: Six AM. Alarm. You survived the night shift.
Except one crew never clocks out. Dust mites. In your pillow, right now.
They eat the flakes of skin you shed every night.
They can't drink. They pull water out of the air, so a humid bedroom is their favorite.
They don't bite. But their droppings are one of the top triggers of allergies and asthma.
And keep the air in your bedroom below fifty percent humidity.
The fix: wash your sheets and pillowcases in hot water every week.
So tonight, when you turn off the light, now you know who's clocking in.
And if you want to know which of them you should actually kill, that one's next.
